[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick roll call — we'll kick off, uh, this is Maya from Redwood, I have Ravi our solutions engineer with me.

[00:10] Marcus Liu: hey

[00:14] Maya: Great. High level, we wanted to map hosting options to the budget and performance constraints you mentioned in the intake form. We're expecting to cover per-token levers like batching and caching, and talk pilot math. Does that align?
[00:26] Olivia: Yes. We're trying to run an assistant that surfaces portfolio summarizations and internal docs search, so queries vary — some are short, some are long. Our ask is to keep p95 under about 250ms for front-line workflows, and ideally monthly spend < $15k for the pilot.
[00:45] Maya: Solid. Can you share current traffic estimates? tokens per request? RPS?
[00:50] Olivia: ballpark: 30k tokens/day aggregated, maybe 1.2k requests/day. Avg prompt ~120 tokens, responses ~250 tokens, but we have bursts from a small set of power users.
[01:07] Ravi Patel: ok that distribution helps. For that shape, batching and prefix K/V caching can drop effective per-token compute by, uh, roughly 20-60% depending on reuse. Quick note: our served runtime supports continuous batching and smart routing which tries to balance latency SLOs.
[01:22] Marcus: when you say smart routing, does that mean some requests might be routed to a slightly smaller model to save cost?
[01:27] Ravi: yes, we have model variants and routing policies. You can set fallback to cheaper variant when Dedicated capacity is saturated, or route by latency sensitivity. But you decide precision vs cost.
[01:37] Sofia: From finance side, we need clear unit economics — if average request is 370 tokens total, what's our per-request cost hosted vs dedicated? We need a return calc.
[01:48] Maya: right, let's walk through a simple worked example. For hosted, our current public rates for the model you're evaluating (open-llm-v2-ish family) are X per 1k input tokens and Y per 1k output tokens — I'll attach the exact sheet. But key levers: batching reduces per-token kernel overhead, KV/prefix cache can remove repeated prompt tokens — think system prompt and document embeddings — and quantization can drop model compute by ~30% on supported hardware.
[02:17] Olivia: can we get that sheet now? Even ballpark numbers are useful.
[02:20] Maya: Absolutely, we'll send the pricing scenarios. For your volume, initial hosted estimate without caching: roughly $9k–12k/month. With prefix cache hit rate of 40% and batching tuned, that moves down to around $6k–8k. Dedicated reserved starts at a higher fixed fee but gives predictability and lowers marginal cost per token if you scale.
[02:38] Marcus: So dedicated is better if we expect to double volume in three months?
[02:42] Ravi: Usually yes. Dedicated reduces per-token variable cost because GPUs are reserved and you avoid some multi-tenant markup. But there's a commit and capacity planning step — we size pools to meet your throughput and p95 targets.
[02:53] Olivia: The tricky bit is we can't commit to big spend ex ante. Pilot budget is strict. Is there a hybrid approach?
[02:59] Maya: Totally. We often run pilots on hosted with a hard cap and then transition to dedicated when you cross a threshold; or we run a short dedicated pilot (1–3 months) with a smaller reserved pool and a buyout/credit toward a longer commit if you adopt. We can structure commercial terms around that.
[03:15] Sofia: That sounds promising but we need contract clarity — what about data residency and KMS? We have some LP data that can't leave certain regions.
[03:23] Ravi: For Private we deploy into your VPC or on-prem where the control plane is private and you hold KMS keys. We also support regionalized hosted options in EMEA and US regions to meet residency. Audit logs and SAML SSO are supported; we can show the SOC2 doc.
[03:37] Marcus: On latency: you mentioned batching, but batching sometimes adds latency for single-user flows. How do you reconcile p95 <250ms with batching?
[03:45] Ravi: Great question. We do continuous batching with latency SLO-aware policies — small 'fast lanes' for latency-critical requests and 'batch lanes' for throughput. You can route by route or token threshold. For example, user-facing assistant calls can go to low-latency pool with smaller batch windows; backend summarization can be batched aggressively.
[04:05] Olivia: Ok. So for the pilot, we want assistant calls in low-latency lane p95<250ms and background processing batched. Budgeted $15k/month — can we simulate that distribution?
[04:19] Maya: Yes. We'll produce two scenarios: conservative (no caching, hosted) and optimized (40% caching, mixture of lanes). Also show dedicated pilot with reserved baseline.
[04:28] Marcus: There's also concern about cold-start KV cache effects — initial rollout often has low hit rates. How do you advise seeding caches?
[04:35] Ravi: We recommend warming strategies: pre-populate KV with top N documents, keep system prompts cached, and for embeddings-backed retrieval, run a background indexing job to pre-cache common prefixes. We'll include runbook suggestions in the follow-up.
[04:49] Sofia: From finance perspective, show worst-case spend if caching fails. We need guardrails and alerts.
[04:55] Maya: We'll include hard budget caps, usage alerts, and automatic fallback to a cheaper model if spend nears threshold. That keeps spend predictable.
[05:03] Marcus: Regarding quantization — does Redwood handle model quantization or do we ship quantized models?
[05:08] Ravi: Our runtime supports multiple quantized formats; we onboard model variants and choose quant kernel per hardware. For private deployments, we can run your quantized artifact. For hosted, we manage quantization and report accuracy/regression.
[05:20] Olivia: Any limitations on sequence length? Some of our long-doc summarizations go to 8k tokens.
[05:26] Ravi: We support long-context families but cost scales roughly linearly with sequence. We also have KV caching for long contexts to reduce repeated context reprocessing — works well when much of the context is stable.
[05:37] Olivia: OK. Can you estimate per-token for a long request? say 8k context in + 1k output.
[05:44] Maya: We'll model that explicitly but expect per-call cost to be severalx higher relative to short calls; caching can mitigate if the 8k is mostly unchanged across requests.
[05:53] Marcus: On SLAs: if latency SLOs are missed due to capacity, what's the escalation and fallback?
[05:58] Ravi: We have automatic routing fallback — requests can be retried to a compatible variant or routed to hosted pool in a different region. For dedicated with an SLA, we commit to capacity and have escalation paths. We'll include our policy in the docs.
[06:12] Sofia: We also need to see predictable reporting per-token and per-route cost breakdown. Our FinOps team will want daily granularity.
[06:19] Maya: Redwood Console provides token-level breakdown, per-route dashboards, and exportable CSVs for daily usage. We'll demo that in the next step.
[06:27] Olivia: For the pilot, what minimum integration effort is typical?
[06:31] Ravi: For the typical stack, integration is an API call and optional agent to prefetch embeddings. We can provide a quickstart that takes your team a couple of days to wire, and our SEs help for deeper infra work. If you want VPC/private, that stretches to 2-4 weeks for deployment and security review.
[06:47] Marcus: Our infra team will want to run a perf test with a replay of production traffic. Can you support that?
[06:50] Ravi: Yes — we can accept replayed traces or a synthetic generator. We also provide guidance for running mlperf-like latency/throughput tests; for dedicated we'd run an on-site/privatedemo.
[07:05] Olivia: Good. Let's discuss pilot KPI: we propose 30 days, $15k budget, p95 < 250ms for assistant lane, and a target cache hit of >30% within 2 weeks. Is that feasible?
[07:17] Maya: That's a reasonable ask to test fit. We'll model scenarios with your input distribution and confirm feasibility. The main risk is the initial cold-cache — we'll recommend a seed plan for first 48 hours.
[07:30] Sofia: Also need to know termination/cutover costs if we move to dedicated.
[07:35] Maya: We can include a credit to apply pilot hosted spend toward a dedicated commit within 90 days. We'll outline options.
[07:44] Marcus: About compliance — we might require a contract clause about data deletion and key escrow. Is that standard?
[07:50] Ravi: We can include deletion guarantees and proof-of-deletion workflow for Private deployments. With customer-managed KMS, keys are under your control.
[07:59] Olivia: Any competitors we should be aware of that have different economics?
[08:03] Maya: Some do per-request flat fees or coarser granularity; others push for longer commitments to reduce unit cost. We'll include a competitor comp table in the deck.
